To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the elderly compared to young subjects execute downward stepping with substantially increased leg stiffness.
the elderly compared to young subjects stiffen the leg by 64% during downward stepping.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biomechanics of the aging locomotor system.
how the neuromusculoskeletal system controls the impact of the lower extremity during downward stepping in young and old adults.
the role of muscle activity in the maintenance of balance and the prevention of falls in elderly people.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the elderly people elevate muscle activity during the pre-contact phase to stiffen the legs in compensation for impaired sensory-motor functions.
the increased leg stiffness in the elderly is associated with increased coactivity of antagonistic muscles during the impact phase and with increased muscle pre-activity preceding the impact.
elderly people stiffen their leg to prevent falling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aging is associated with reduced neuromotor control, which is compensated for by increased muscle coactivity and pre-activation to stiffen the limb.
aging is associated with reduced muscle strength, increased neuromuscular fatigue, and reduced neuromotor control.

aging leads to a reduction in the ability to modulate leg stiffness in response to a perturbation, but the elderly can still stiffen the limb to some extent by increasing muscle pre- and/or coactivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the elderly elevate muscle activity to stiffen the limb in compensation for impaired motor control functions.
elderly people elevate muscle activity during downward stepping to compensate for impaired neuromuscular functions.
elderly people stiffen their legs by increasing muscle coactivity during downward step landing.
